analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers and public programs to cover HIV-prevention drugs free of charge and funds access for the uninsured.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the Senate and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require nearly every kind of health coverage — private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service — to pay the full cost of drugs that prevent HIV, with no copays, deductibles, or preauthorization, and would cover the lab tests and follow-up visits those drugs require. It would also create grant programs so uninsured and underinsured people can get the drugs for free, ban insurers from denying life, disability, or long-term care coverage to people taking HIV-prevention medication, and fund a public education campaign. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee it was sent to, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.2 million Americans the CDC estimates could benefit from PrEP, only about 31% of whom filled a prescription in 2022 [S3]. Black, Latino, and female patients — who were prescribed PrEP at rates of 11%, 21%, and under 12% of eligible people in 2022, versus 82% of eligible White people — gain most, because the bill forces coverage regardless of cost, prior approval, or insurer discretion [S3]. Uninsured and underinsured people gain through direct grant-funded access, and survivors of sexual assault gain faster access to emergency PEP without preauthorization hurdles [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of HIV, especially uninsured and low-income patients

how_it_helps.text: Requires private plans, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, FEHB, TRICARE, VA, and Indian Health Service to cover HIV-prevention drugs, lab work, and follow-up visits with no copays, deductibles, or preauthorization.

Creates grant programs for states, tribes, and community clinics to pay for PrEP and PEP for people without adequate insurance, plus a CDC public-education campaign targeting communities where prevention drugs are underused.
Makes it unlawful for life, disability, or long-term care insurers to deny coverage or raise premiums because someone takes HIV-prevention medication.
Adds a private right of action so patients can sue insurers that violate the coverage rules, with attorney fees for prevailing plaintiffs, and requires annual insurer compliance reporting to HHS.

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers, who must cover the drugs, testing, and follow-up with no cost-sharing and no preauthorization, and must report compliance data and face enforcement by three federal agencies plus private lawsuits [S2, S3]. Life, disability, and long-term care insurers lose the ability to deny or reprice policies for people on prevention medication [S2]. Taxpayers fund the grant programs and education campaigns, which are authorized at unspecified sums [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and, for grants, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The mandate that insurers cover all HIV-prevention drugs, lab work, and follow-up with no cost-sharing, and the ban on preauthorization, shifts those costs onto premiums for everyone with private insurance.

The grant programs for uninsured and underinsured people are authorized at 'such sums as are necessary,' an open-ended federal spending commitment with no fixed dollar limit for fiscal years 2024 through 2029.

The bill also bars life, disability, and long-term care insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums based on a person taking HIV-prevention medication, which insurers argue limits their ability to price risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: free PrEP and PEP for tens of thousands of people, fewer new HIV infections (each of which costs hundreds of thousands of dollars in lifetime treatment), and a fix for insurers quietly charging or denying people who take prevention medication. The costs fall on insurers and drugmakers through lost cost-sharing revenue and mandated coverage, and on taxpayers through the grant program, which authorizes unspecified sums. The main design weakness is the open-ended funding authorization and the breadth of "related services... without limitation," which makes long-term cost estimates difficult. On balance, the public-health and equity benefits plainly outweigh those costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 22, 2023 by Senator Tina Smith and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
It attracted only one cosponsor in the Senate, a Democrat, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the House, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without it advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, who avoided new no-cost coverage mandates and enforcement, and life, disability, and long-term care insurers, who kept the ability to price and deny coverage based on PrEP use. People at risk of HIV got nothing from this bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, who avoided the coverage mandates

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full text in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration, leaving it without a mark-up or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a vote, so no roll-call split exists; both sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill requires them to cover all HIV-prevention drugs and related services with no cost-sharing, bans preauthorization, and exposes them to patient lawsuits and federal compliance enforcement. Their interest ran directly against the bill.

industries.industry: Brand-name and generic drug makers selling HIV-prevention drugs
industries.note: Guaranteed no-cost coverage and public grants would expand the number of prescriptions filled, including for expensive brand-name products. Their interest aligned with expanded access, which is why this entrenchment is worth noting alongside the public benefit.

industries.industry: Life, disability, and long-term care insurers
industries.note: They would be barred from denying coverage or charging higher premiums to people taking HIV-prevention medication, eliminating a screening practice they used to price these policies.

industries.industry: Community health centers and HIV service organizations
industries.note: Federally qualified health centers, family planning grantees, and community clinics are directly eligible for new federal grants to fund PrEP and PEP services, outreach, and patient navigators.
